claimed.text: Lazar alleges, in his 1991 narration, that he was bussed to S-4 from near Groom Lake, that he was paid by the Navy for the duration of the work, and that his Los Alamos job is the most easily verifiable of his clearances. The tape is evidence of what he claims and never of its content.

Lazar's physical claim, on the same tape, is that in the heavier stable elements a gravity wave he calls gravity A extends past the perimeter of the atom, and that gravity A is what mainstream physics calls the strong nuclear force.

Lazar says he met Edward Teller in Los Alamos in 1982 on the day the newspaper ran his jet-car story, later wrote to him about a job, and was referred on by telephone. No opened record corroborates this, and the board carries it at Tier 3 as only what Lazar said.

Gene Huff, a Las Vegas real-estate appraiser who met Lazar in 1985 and was his friend by 1988, is a witness to lights, not to a facility: he places three desert viewings on 22 March, 29 March and 5 April 1989, the last ending when guards found the group and the Lincoln County Sheriff detained them. He also recalls a cheque for $958.11 and says Lazar's W-2 matched it; the form was not opened.

Huff replied in May 1995 that the probation officer misunderstood the Pacifica entry, saying Lazar had taken only an English course and a history course there by correspondence. The board carries the rebuttal beside the report and does not adopt it.

John Lear, whose own dated claim statement of 29 December 1987 precedes Lazar's appearance by about eighteen months, had met Lazar by 1988 and was present at two of the three 1989 viewings. He is a carrier of the claim, not an eyewitness to the site, and nothing the board opened says he introduced Lazar to Knapp.

How it reached air rests, for now, on a secondary chronology: Tom Mahood's timeline has Knapp interviewing Lazar from March 1989, silhouetted interviews under the pseudonym Dennis airing in May 1989, and a named interview in November 1989. No 1989 broadcast artefact has been opened, and the board holds these dates at Tier 3.
Tim McMillan reports that discussion of the 2017 search in the 2018 documentary is what prompted his records request, making the film the route by which the search entered the UFO literature.

contested.text: The credential case against Lazar was made by a UFO proponent. Stanton Friedman found no diplomas, transcripts or yearbook pages, and found that the professor Lazar named as a Caltech instructor taught at Pierce Junior College, where Lazar had taken at least one of his classes.

Tom Mahood, a physics graduate who spent years on the record, concludes that Lazar never attended Caltech or MIT; his investigation records that a 1993 search found no Lazar in any MIT student directory from 1978 to 1990, and that Caltech says it has never had a graduate degree in electronics.

The Los Alamos directory page that carries Lazar's name, as Friedman describes it, covers DOE employees and the outside contractor Kirk-Mayer; a Los Alamos colleague said on tape in 1996 that Lazar was a contractor; and Huff himself records a Kirk-Mayer employee number and that the laboratory and Kirk-Mayer later said they held no employment records for him. Mahood concludes he was an electronic technician for Kirk-Mayer.

Aerial photographs taken on an authorised flight over Papoose Lake, published by Tyler Rogoway, show nothing on the lakebed and no access road. The board's own search found no opened government record naming a facility called S-4 at Papoose Lake, which it states as a negative finding, not proof of absence.

Two people reach the same counter-explanation by unrelated routes: Mahood and T.D. Barnes, a former engineer at Groom Lake, both say the designator S-4 belongs to a radar facility on the Tonopah side of the range. Mahood argues the account began as a cover story after security caught Lazar bringing friends to watch classified tests in April 1989, while conceding that Lazar is "amazingly believable".

Nothing about the synthesised element 115 is stable, machinable, storable or available in gram quantities, which directly contradicts the claim's central requirement without refuting the element's existence. The physicist David Morgan adds that the strong force has nothing to do with gravity, that its range does not grow with nuclear mass, and that antimatter made on board yields no net energy.

Mahood's research shows the island of stability near element 114 was published popular physics from 1969, which cuts against the credulous reading and the hostile one alike: the idea was available before 1989.

The payment claim does not agree with itself. Lazar's narration says the Navy paid him; the W-2 as Friedman describes it names a Department of Naval Intelligence, which is not an entity that exists, and totals under $1000. The board has not opened the form.

The Teller anecdote is misdated on its own terms: Lazar puts the newspaper story and Teller's speech on the same day, while the article is dated 27 June 1982 and Mahood puts the lecture on the following day.

The 2017 search is widely retold as a seizure of alien fuel; the police record ties it to a thallium poisoning inquiry in Houghton, Michigan, in which Lazar is not recorded as a suspect. The federal fireworks matter is likewise often told as Lazar's own guilty plea, when the primary release says the company pled guilty.

lead.text: Bob Lazar says that between December 1988 and April 1989 he worked at a facility he calls S-4, about fifteen miles south of Area 51 at Groom Lake, where he says he saw nine discs, and he describes a reactor fuelled by element 115. The account reached the public through KLAS-TV in 1989 and his own 1991 videotape; the court file, the credential checks and the real element 115 all cut against it.

record.text: The Los Alamos Monitor of 27 June 1982, in a front-page story about a jet-powered Honda Lazar had built, described him in its own voice as a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility. The board carries that description as what he told the reporter, not as an employment record.

Lazar's Pre-Sentence Report of 27 July 1990, produced for the Clark County court after his guilty plea, lists his reported education as a 1978 physics and electronic technology degree from Pacifica University, a 1982 physics master's from MIT and a 1985 electronic technology master's from Caltech. It shows what he reported about himself to a court.

He was arrested for pandering in Las Vegas on 5 June 1990, pleaded guilty on 18 June 1990 and was sentenced on 20 August 1990 by District Judge Jack Lehman to probation, community service and psychotherapy, the judge saying he "could not make a determination regarding his claims". A 1996 petition to withdraw the plea was denied, and the conviction stands.

The Las Vegas Review-Journal of 19 June 1990 recorded that Lazar was the focal point of much of Knapp's award-winning KLAS-TV series, and recorded from police records that he had told the woman in the case he held master's degrees from two universities.

The claim's geography moved on the contemporaneous record. The Review-Journal of 21 August 1990 described Lazar's claim as being that the government was testing alien spacecraft at the Nevada Test Site, 65 miles northwest of Las Vegas, a Department of Energy site rather than the Air Force range where the account later settled.
The 1991 tape survives as an Internet Archive item: forty minutes, created by Gene Huff and Bob Lazar and published by Tri-Dot Productions, with video formats only and no transcript.

The real element 115 was first reported by a Dubna and Lawrence Livermore collaboration in Physical Review C on 2 February 2004, from decay chains that ran to completion within seconds. IUPAC assigned discovery priority on 30 December 2015 on work from 2010 to 2013, and the name moscovium was approved on 28 November 2016.

A Laingsburg, Michigan police report, obtained by Tim McMillan under a state open-records request, records an agency assist on 19 July 2017 supporting an FBI search of Lazar's business United Nuclear Scientific in aid of a homicide investigation involving poison, and records that Lazar gave permission for the search. The Black Vault reports that the FBI denies its United Nuclear file holds records of that raid.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission's release of 20 July 2007 records that United Nuclear Scientific Supplies, founded and operated by Lazar, pled guilty to three criminal counts and was fined $7,500 with three years probation, while Lazar himself appears in a separate civil consent decree limiting sales of fireworks-related chemicals.

The 2018 documentary Bob Lazar: Area 51 and Flying Saucers runs 97 minutes, was directed by Jeremy Corbell and features Lazar, George Knapp and Joy White. Its listing gives three release dates across two territories, the first being United States digital on 1 November 2018.

summary.text: In his own narration on a 1991 videotape, Lazar claims he held secret and above top secret clearances, worked at S-4 on the Nellis Air Force range between December 1988 and April 1989, was paid by the United States Navy, saw a hangar complex built into a mountain with nine angled doors, and had at least partial views of nine different discs. The captions the board read are machine-generated, so the wording is approximate.

The same tape carries the fuel claim: that stable superheavy elements exist in the 114 to 115 range, that a reactor uses element 115 as its fuel, that 223 grams would last twenty to thirty years, and that the element is machined into triangles and inserted into the reactor.

The claim travelled by three carriers: George Knapp's KLAS-TV series, of which a June 1990 newspaper says Lazar was the focal point; the 1991 tape, written and co-produced by his friend Gene Huff; and Jeremy Corbell's 2018 documentary, which returned the claim to mass circulation.

The topic sets the account beside the records that bear on it: a Nevada court file that carries his own reported credentials, the checks of those credentials, the aerial state of Papoose Lake, and the synthesis of the real element 115.
